playful-poems: Henry Morley, a Victorian professor better known for serious scholarship, lets his lighter side out in this verse collection. The poems are witty, rhymed, and meant to amuse — literary jokes, parodies, and cheerful nonsense rather than heavy themes. Readers looking for poetry that smiles will find Morley an agreeable companion, learned but never stuffy.
sociology-and-modern-social-problems: Sociologist Charles Ellwood wrote this early textbook to show how the new science of sociology could address poverty, crime, and family breakdown. Each chapter takes a pressing social problem of the 1910s and examines its causes with calm, scientific care. The book helped establish sociology as a serious field aimed at making society better, not just describing it.
the-coming-of-the-princess-and-other-poe: Canadian poet Kate Seymour MacLean gathers lyrics on love, nature, and imagination, led by the title poem's fairy-tale romance. Her verse carries the refined, musical manner of late-Victorian poetry. A graceful collection from a writer who brought a delicate touch to Canada's early literature.
old-spookses-pass-malcolm-s-katie-and-ot: Isabella Valancy Crawford — one of Canada's finest early poets — gathers her narrative poems of frontier life and love. Malcolm's Katie, her masterpiece, tells a backwoods love story in vigorous verse. Crawford's work glows with the energy of a young nation finding its voice.
songs-of-labor-and-other-poems: Morris Rosenfeld — the great Yiddish poet of the sweatshops — sings of the suffering and dignity of immigrant workers. His verses gave voice to the men and women bent over sewing machines on New York's Lower East Side. Powerful, heartbreaking poetry from the heart of the labor movement.
canada-and-other-poems: Thomas Frederick Young's verses celebrate Canada — its landscapes, its history, its promise — alongside lyrics on universal themes of love and faith. A patriotic voice from the young Dominion's literary springtime. Sincere, musical, and full of love for the northern land.
fleurs-de-lys-and-other-poems: Arthur Weir's verses, French-Canadian in flavor, sing of history, faith, and the St. Lawrence. His lyrics carry the lilt of old France in the New World. A graceful minor poet of the Dominion's early days. His lines honor the French past of Canada and the quiet beauty of the St. Lawrence valley.
rose-and-roof-tree-poems: George Parsons Lathrop's poems of home and love — the rose and the roof-tree — sing in the high Victorian manner. His lyrics of domestic happiness and quiet faith charmed the readers of his day. Graceful verse from a gifted man of letters.
london-films: William Dean Howells gathers his sketches of London — the streets, the fog, the people — under the novel title of London Films, snapshots of the great city. His gentle, observant eye finds poetry in the everyday. A charming American view of Victorian London.
laura-secord-the-heroine-of-1812-a-drama: Sarah Anne Curzon dramatizes Laura Secord's famous walk through the night to warn the British in 1813. Her verse play honors Canada's heroine, with other poems added. A patriotic work from a pioneering Canadian writer. Her thirty-kilometre walk through enemy woods became a Canadian legend.
dreams-and-days-poems: George Parsons Lathrop's Dreams and Days gathers poems of aspiration and reflection. His cultivated verse pleased the readers of his time. Graceful work from a man of letters. Aspiration and memory mingle in these polished, thoughtful verses. A cultivated American voice, now half-forgotten but worth hearing.
home-lyrics-a-book-of-poems: Hannah Battersby's Home Lyrics sing of domestic joys and sorrows in gentle verse. Her poems graced many a Victorian parlor. Tender, old-fashioned, and sincere. Cradle songs and fireside musings fill this modest, heartfelt book. Her gentle rhymes soothed many a Victorian home.
the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendell-hol: Poems from the Breakfast Table gathers the verse Holmes scattered through his famous Atlantic essays — the Autocrat's table talk in rhyme. Witty, wise, and warmly human, they are the perfect companion to the prose classics. Morning wisdom in musical form.

Poems of the Class of '29 collects Holmes' Harvard reunion verses — half a century of class poems, by turns gay and grave. His loyalty to old classmates shines in every stanza. A touching record of lifelong friendship in rhyme. Classmates long parted meet again in these affectionate lines.

Poems from the Teacups Series collects the verse Holmes wrote for his last Atlantic series — musings over the teacups, charming and wise. The old Autocrat takes his final bow in fragrant company. A last, delightful cup with a beloved friend.
confessions-and-criticisms: Julian Hawthorne, son of the great romancer, sets down his confessions and criticisms — open talk about books, writers, and his own checkered literary life. He praises and blames with gusto, sparing neither friends nor foes. Lively, headstrong literary chat from a born storyteller.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AdamsPerry_Vick: Vickie Adams worked in the Texas School Book Depository and became a witness in the Kennedy assassination. She said she ran down the building's back stairs moments after the shots, a point researchers have argued over ever since. This file holds the government material filed under her name in the assassination records. It is kept as issued, part of the witness paper trail that investigators of the case still work through today.
govdocs-archive_org-vaticancodesystems_V:
American codebreakers studied the Vatican's secret writing during the Second World War. The result was a 1944 cryptanalytic text on Vatican code systems, later reprinted by Aegean Park Press.

The study explains how papal codes were built and how an analyst should attack them: their alphabets, their habits, and their weak points. It treats the Holy See as what it was in wartime, a neutral power whose traffic every capital wanted to read. For students of cryptology, the manual is a rare look at professional codebreaking aimed at one of the world's oldest diplomatic services.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_afghanis:
When the United States negotiated with the Taliban, officials claimed the movement would break with al Qaeda. Newly Published Documents Cast Doubt on Claims Taliban Will Give Up al Qaeda tests that promise against the record.

The briefing book publishes documents that cut against the hopeful claim, drawn from the long history of ties between the two groups. Its method is the Archive's standard one: put the paper in public and let it argue. For readers following the Afghan settlement, the collection is a check on official optimism, grounded in documents rather than commentary.
podcast-dannyjones-UpFqkpiOAMs:
Producer Dan Farah made a documentary on UFO disclosure featuring senior officials. He joins Danny Jones to argue that President Trump's rush to release UFO files has a real reason behind it. Farah lays that reason out. His account centers on what officials have told him privately about the phenomenon and the pressure building around it.

Farah speaks as a man who has sat with the generals and intelligence figures his film assembled, and he reports their seriousness as the story. Jones presses him on what disclosure would actually contain. The claims remain officials' alleged private views, unverifiable here, and Farah's presentation is preserved as such. Listeners following the disclosure saga get its best-connected advocate explaining the endgame he expects, and the political clock he says is driving it.
podcast-tuckercarlson-677g2SsetMs:
Economist Jeffrey Sachs warns Tucker Carlson about forces pushing President Trump toward war with Iran. Sachs, a Columbia professor and longtime UN adviser, has become a fierce critic of American foreign policy. He also addresses the Ukraine and Russia war and its latest escalation.

Sachs argues that a permanent war lobby in Washington steers presidents toward conflict. He traces the Ukraine war to NATO expansion and broken promises, as he sees it. Carlson asks what Trump can do to resist the pressure. Concerned viewers hear a veteran insider's warning from the edge of the establishment.
podcast-tuckercarlson-6gmdh5DxfMs:
Activist Charlie Kirk joins Tucker Carlson to discuss Christian values under attack, the death of JFK, and how Trump changed politics forever. Kirk founded Turning Point USA and built a youth movement on campuses. His youthful fire fills this talk with his mentor Carlson.

Kirk argues that faith is the front line of the country's cultural war. He shares his reading of the Kennedy assassination and the distrust it seeded. The pair trace how Trump remade the Republican Party in ways that cannot be undone. Young and faithful viewers get the activist's full take from a flagship conversation.
podcast-dannyjones-4YKsRXMT9Ms:
Street reporter Luke reports from a Tampa protest for Danny Jones's show. Armed officers stand close behind him as he works. He moves fast to ask marchers why they came.

One protester says she marches for Black lives and against police force. Others share anger, hope, and fear in short bursts. The tape captures noise, tension, and the feel of the street. No studio guest appears; the crowd itself is the subject. The episode preserves a raw slice of protest-era Florida as participants explained themselves in their own words. The fear near the police line feels close and real.
podcast-tuckercarlson-6kGowc9TTms:
Tucker Carlson recalls the day a candidate was shot in the face on camera. Five months later, he says, no true accounting has come. The shooter died, the world moved on, and the story vanished.

Federalist writer Sean Davis was on the case from the start. The title promises an update on the Trump shooting. It also charges that Congress refuses to probe for a reason. Davis and Carlson ask who the shooter was and how he got close. The episode demands answers that officials have not given. Silence from officials hangs over the whole talk.
tibullus-elegies-williams:
Tibullus, a Roman knight of the Augustan age, wrote love elegies that prize the quiet farm over the camp and the court. Theodore Chickering Williams turned the whole Corpus Tibullianum into English verse. The four books gather poems by Tibullus and by hands in his circle.

Delia rules the first book and Nemesis the second, while the poet dreams of a small farm and a faithful hearth. Later books sing of Messalla, his patron, and of Sulpicia, a woman poet of the house. Tibullus is the soft third voice of Latin love elegy, beside Propertius and Ovid. His longing for the countryside still reads fresh.
heckewelder-history-manners-customs:
John Heckewelder was a Moravian missionary who spent forty years among Native peoples. His History, Manners, and Customs of the Indian Nations came out in 1818. The Lenape, or Delaware, stand at the center of his warm account.

Heckewelder describes councils, speech, war, and peace from long close contact. He defends his Native friends against the slurs of white writers. His respect and love for the people mark every chapter he wrote. Few early books on the Lenape are so humane or so full. Generations of readers have treated it as a classic of its kind.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-willem: This biographical entry profiles Pierre Willems, a Belgian Jesuit scholar of the 1800s, tracing his career, his Bollandist labors, and his place as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's Jesuit gallery, preserved among its Bollandist hagiographers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pius-bonifaci: Pius Gams was the Benedictine whose histories mapped the Church's past. This entry covers his career, his Series Episcoporum, and his scholarship. The annalist of the German abbeys: his learned lists ordered the long bishops' succession of medieval Germany faithfully.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-psalms: The Psalms are the prayer book of Israel and the Church. This long entry treats their authorship, their kinds, and their use. The hymns of David: their holy verses fill the daily Office of the Church worldwide in song and prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reims: Reims became the archdiocese of the coronation city. This entry covers its archbishops, its cathedral, and its history. The city where kings were anointed: its holy ampulla held the sacred chrism of Clovis's baptism in 496's cold winter of faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rudolf-von-em: Rudolf von Ems was the courtly poet of the chronicles. This entry notes his Alexander, his Willehalm, and his art. The versifier of the Hohenstaufen court: his courtly rhymes told of Alexander the Great in German verse of the 1240s.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-synods-of-rei: The Synods of Reims were the councils of Champagne. This entry traces their canons and their history. The assemblies of the French church: their solemn canons crowned Reims in the 800s' Champagne in the Vesle of the very old river.
anne-s-house-of-dreams: Newly married Anne and Gilbert settle into their first home at Four Winds in this fifth Anne of Green Gables book. Joy turns to grief when their first baby dies. Anne finds comfort in two neighbors: Captain Jim, an old sailor writing his life story, and Leslie Moore, a beautiful woman trapped in a cruel marriage. Tender and sad by turns, it is the most emotional volume of the series.
the-chinese-nightingale-and-other-poems: Poems by Vachel Lindsay, the American "singing poet" who chanted his verses like jazz and gospel. The title piece retells Hans Christian Andersen's tale of the emperor and the nightingale, while others celebrate railroads, revival meetings, and the American heartland in bouncing, musical rhythms. Lindsay performed his work across the country, and these pages still carry the beat of his voice.
poems: Poems by Alan Seeger, the young American who joined the French Foreign Legion and was killed in World War I at twenty-eight. His verses blend classical beauty with a soldier's clear-eyed acceptance of death, above all in "I Have a Rendezvous with Death," his most famous poem. Published after he fell in 1916, the collection is the voice of a lost generation's brightest promise.
phantasmagoria-and-other-poems: Lewis Carroll's comic verse at its most playful, led by the title poem: a chatty ghost explains haunting to the man whose house he occupies. The rest of the volume mixes parody, wordplay, and gentle nonsense in Carroll's unmistakable style. Readers who know only Alice will enjoy meeting Carroll the poet, sly and musical and full of surprises.
moral-emblems: Stevenson's book of verses paired with woodcut illustrations, a playful experiment in matching pictures to poems. Short, catchy, and often comic, the emblems show his lighter side, far from the adventure novels. A curiosity for Stevenson lovers, it reveals the craftsman amusing himself between greater works.
ballads-and-lyrics-of-old-france-with-ot: Andrew Lang's translations of medieval French ballads and songs, including the work of Villon and Charles of Orléans. Rendered into graceful English verse, these poems of love, exile, and gallows humor sing across six centuries. Lang the fairy-tale collector shows here his other gift: bringing old poetry back to life.
dreams: Jerome K. Jerome turns his comic eye to the strange logic of dreams in this short humorous piece. With the same chatty warmth as Three Men in a Boat, he recounts absurd nighttime adventures and the embarrassment of telling them at breakfast. Light and brief, it is Jerome doing what he did best: finding philosophy in silliness.
alice-adams: Booth Tarkington's Pulitzer Prize novel about Alice Adams, a small-town girl hungry for a grander life than her family can afford. Her social climbing, built on pretension and a mother's scheming, leads to humiliation and a hard-won honesty. Published in 1921, it is a sharp, sympathetic portrait of American ambition and its costs.
the-congo-and-other-poems: Vachel Lindsay's 1914 collection, famous for the title poem's drumming rhythms about Africa, meant to be chanted aloud. Lindsay's "singing poetry" mixed jazz-age energy with missionary-era imagery, in verses both thrilling and troubling to modern ears. A landmark of performance poetry and a document of its time.
charmides-and-other-poems: Oscar Wilde's early poems, published in 1881, lush with classical myth and Pre-Raphaelite beauty. "Charmides" tells a sensual Greek legend in flowing verse, while the shorter pieces show a young aesthete intoxicated by art. Imitative but gorgeous, they are the apprenticeship of a genius finding his voice.
a-reading-of-life-with-other-poems: Poems by George Meredith, the Victorian novelist whose verse is as vigorous as his fiction. Philosophical, musical, and deeply engaged with nature and modern thought, these poems reward careful reading. Less known than his novels but admired by poets, they show Meredith's formidable mind at play.
new-poems: More poems by Francis Thompson, continuing his quest for the divine in ornate, musical verse. Ecstatic and melancholy by turns, they show his unique vision undimmed. For readers who cherish religious poetry of the highest ambition.
extracts-from-adam-s-diary-translated-fr: Mark Twain's 1904 comic diary of Adam in the Garden of Eden: his puzzlement over Eve, the Fall, and family life. Tender and hilarious by turns, it is Twain at his most human. A small masterpiece of humor.
mazelli-and-other-poems: Poems by George Sands, including the title piece Mazelli. Romantic and earnest in the mid-Victorian manner, they show a minor poet's sincere craft. Period verse for collectors of the era's poetry. Sands sings of love and nature with a true, if modest, voice.
the-education-of-henry-adams: Henry Adams's 1907 autobiography: the education of an American aristocrat from the Civil War to the dynamo age. Ironic, brilliant, and deeply pessimistic, it is the great American memoir. A Pulitzer winner and a landmark of introspection.
the-formation-of-vegetable-mould-through: Darwin's 1881 book on earthworms: how worms make vegetable mould and shape the earth. The great naturalist's last work, patient and delightful, finds grandeur in the humblest creatures. Science at its most charming and profound. Darwin's worms turn the earth, and his book turns our view of nature.
love-or-fame-and-other-poems: Fannie Isabelle Sherrick's poems of love or fame: verses of sentiment and ambition. Earnest and musical in the popular style, they pleased their readers. Period American poetry. Sherrick's verses sing of the heart's choices between love and fame.
many-voices-poems: Nesbit's Many Voices: poems for children and grown-ups alike. Charming, musical, and full of her warm imagination, they show the novelist as poet. A delightful collection. Nesbit's verse is as warm as her stories.
a-defence-of-poesie-and-poems: Philip Sidney's Defence of Poesie: the great Elizabethan argument for poetry, with his poems beside it. Eloquent and noble, it founded English criticism. The poet as prophet and teacher. Sidney's argument ennobles all poets, the poet as prophet.
yorkshire-dialect-poems-1673-1915-and-tr: Frederic Moorman's Yorkshire dialect poems: two and a half centuries of northern verse. The dales' own voice, rough and musical. A unique anthology. The dales speak in their own tongue, northern verse anthologized, a unique anthology.
forty-two-poems: James Elroy Flecker's Forty-Two Poems: the golden journey to Samarkand. The early-modern poet's exotic verse, brilliant and brief. "We are the pilgrims, master.", flecker's golden road runs to Samarkand, the young poet's exotic music, brief and bright, a talent lost too soon.
music-and-other-poems: Henry Van Dyke's Music and Other Poems: the beloved poet's verse. Nature and faith in song. Gentle and musical. A fine collection, van Dyke's gentle verse, nature and faith, a fine collection, Henry Van Dyke.
love-at-arms: Rafael Sabatini spins Love-at-Arms, a swashbuckling romance set in old Italy. A gallant hero fights for honor and for the woman he loves. Duels, plots, and narrow escapes fill every chapter. A thrilling ride for lovers of adventure.
maurine-and-other-poems: Ella Wheeler Wilcox's Maurine and Other Poems sings of love and fate. The long title romance unfolds in smooth and flowing verse. Warm sentiment and sweet melody carry along every page. Popular poetry written straight from the heart.
aretaeus-extant-works-adams:
Francis Adams translated the Extant Works of Aretaeus the Cappadocian in 1856. Aretaeus practiced medicine around 150 CE in the Roman Empire. Posterity ranks him the finest clinical observer of antiquity.

His descriptions of diabetes, asthma, epilepsy, and tetanus remain classics. He watches symptoms closely and writes them down with literary power. Diabetes receives its classic portrait here, thirst and wasting included. Adams kept the exact Greek sense in careful English prose. Little is known of Aretaeus's life beyond these surviving books. Clinical medicine before the name existed is what his pages show. Physicians still quote his disease portraits with respect. His eye was sharp and his pen was just as sharp.
grand-grimoire-1750-ms:
Before print fixed the Red Dragon's shape, the Grand Grimoire circulated in handwriting. This manuscript version dates to about 1750. It is an earlier redaction of the pact grimoire, textually distinct from the nineteenth-century printed editions that made the book famous across France.

The famous bargain with Lucifuge stands here in a less settled form. Scribes copied such books for buyers who could pay, changing details as they went. Comparing this draft-stage text with the printed Dragon shows the tradition in motion. The manuscript is the grimoire's own early state, before editors and printers froze it. Students of the French black books prize witnesses of exactly this kind.
doe-osti-3022998-georgetown-university-s: Written for a Georgetown graduate course in systems engineering, this report covers integration, verification, and validation — the discipline of making sure complex systems' parts work together and do what they were asked to do. It walks through the methods engineers use to test whole systems. A solid classroom treatment of a real-world engineering skill.
nasa-tm-19670027698-the-analysis-of-tops: Satellites looking down at Earth see the ionosphere's top side. This 1967 NASA report covers the analysis of topside ionograms — the echo traces those satellites record. The methods turned squiggles into maps of charged particles above us.

Attributed mostly to King David, the Psalms have been prayed and sung for three thousand years. This 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation gives the Hebrew poetry in English shaped by a committee of Jewish scholars.
